opus-5.5.text:
I think tool use is actually one of the most underrated pieces of the puzzle. When people talk about AGI understanding the physical world, there's often an assumption that a big enough neural network will just absorb physics from data, from videos, from text. And to some extent that works. You can get models that produce very plausible-looking motion. But plausible-looking isn't the same as correct, and in physics the difference really matters.

My background is in physical simulation and computer graphics, so I've spent a lot of time thinking about this. We have centuries of accumulated knowledge about how the physical world works: conservation laws, partial differential equations, numerical methods that are very precise and very efficient. It would be strange to ask a neural network to rediscover all of that implicitly inside its weights, approximately, and at enormous cost. It's a bit like asking a person to do fluid dynamics in their head instead of letting them use a computer.

So the way I see it, an intelligent system should do what a good scientist or engineer does. It should have intuition, a rough mental model of what's going to happen, but when precision matters, it should reach for the right tool. That might be a simulator, a differentiable physics engine, a solver, or even just writing and running some code. The model's job is to set up the problem correctly, choose the right abstraction, interpret the results, and notice when something looks wrong.

That's also part of why I care so much about making simulation tools easier to program and faster to run. If physics tools are hard to use, neither humans nor AI systems will use them well. If they become accessible, expressive, and fast, then they become a natural extension of reasoning. An AI could form a hypothesis, simulate it, compare against observations, and refine its understanding in a loop. That's much closer to how real understanding works.

And there's a nice two-way relationship here. Differentiable simulators let you backpropagate through physics, so learning systems and physical models can be combined rather than treated as competitors. The learned part handles what's messy and hard to model explicitly, and the physics part provides structure and guarantees.

So I wouldn't say tool use is a shortcut or a crutch. I'd say it's a big part of what intelligence is. Humans didn't become good at understanding the physical world just by having bigger brains. We built instruments, math, and computers. I expect AGI will be similar: its understanding of physics will come from combining learned intuition with very powerful, very precise tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this question a lot, because my whole background is in physical simulation, and it changed how I see what intelligence actually is.

Here is the honest observation. Humans don't understand physics by looking at the world and intuiting equations. We understand it by building instruments. Galileo rolled balls down inclined planes because the free fall was too fast to perceive. Newton needed calculus, which is itself a tool, a kind of cognitive prosthetic. Every real leap in understanding the physical world came paired with a new instrument or a new mathematical machine.

So when people ask whether a language model can "understand" physics by reading all of the textbooks, my answer is: not fully, and that's fine, because neither can a human. The textbook is the compressed residue of thousands of experiments. The understanding lives in the loop between hypothesis and measurement, and tools are what close that loop.

For an AGI, I see three kinds of tools that matter.

The first is simulation. A differentiable physics engine, a fluid solver, a finite element code. These let a model run experiments at a rate and scale no physical lab can match. If I want to know whether a bridge design fails, I don't need intuition, I need to run the solver. And crucially, a good simulator gives the model a ground truth that is independent of its own training data. That's the thing that stops it from hallucinating confidently about the physical world.

The second is symbolic and numerical computation. The model's weights are very good at pattern completion and very bad at arithmetic over twenty steps. Handing it a computer algebra system or a numerical library is like handing a brilliant physicist a calculator. Nobody thinks less of the physicist.

The third is the real world itself, through sensors and actuators. Simulation is always wrong somewhere. The sim-to-real gap is a humbling thing when you work in robotics. So eventually the model has to be able to poke the world and get surprised. Surprise is where learning happens.

What excites me is the architecture that emerges from this. The model becomes the scientist, and the tools become the laboratory. The model's job is to pose good questions, interpret results, and notice when something doesn't fit. That's actually what we value in human physicists. We don't admire them for mentally integrating Navier-Stokes. We admire them for knowing which experiment to run.

I'll add one caution. Tool use only helps understanding if the model is actually using the tool to update its beliefs, not just to decorate an answer it already decided on. I've seen systems call a solver and then ignore the output because it contradicted the prior. That's not understanding, that's theater. The hard research problem isn't giving models tools. It's making them genuinely accountable to what the tools return.

So, to summarize: I don't think tool use is a crutch on the way to AGI understanding physics. I think it is the understanding. The instrument and the mind have always been one system.

astra-6.text:
I think tool use is very important because it gives an AI a way to test its understanding. You can learn descriptions of physical phenomena from text, but predicting what will happen in a particular situation requires more than repeating those descriptions.

For example, an AI could use a physics simulator to ask, “If I change this object's shape or this material property, what happens?” It can make a prediction, run an experiment, and compare the result with its prediction. That creates a feedback loop where tools help it develop and refine models of the world.

But a simulator is also an approximation. The AI needs to understand its assumptions and eventually check predictions against real observations. So I see tools as a bridge between reasoning and experimentation. The important capability is knowing what experiment to run, what the result tells you, and when your model needs to change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tool use is very important, because understanding physics is more than being able to describe it in language. You want an AI to make a prediction, run an experiment, observe the result, and revise its understanding.

A physics simulator can support that loop. The AI can change a material property or an initial condition and ask, “What happens if I do this?” It can test many hypotheses much faster than it could with physical experiments alone.

But using a simulator doesn’t automatically mean the AI understands the world. Every simulator makes assumptions. The deeper capability is knowing which tool to use, what its limitations are, and when you need a real-world measurement. I see tools as a way to connect reasoning with evidence. That connection is essential if we want AI to reason reliably about physical phenomena.
